studies.introduction: The Psalms provide believers with a rich biblical framework for worship, prayer, trust, repentance and righteous living. They reveal that a genuine relationship with God involves more than public religious activities or joyful expressions of praise. It includes honest lament during distress, confidence in God's justice, dependence on His protection, submission to His Word, repentance from sin and commitment to holiness. Psalms 6–28 present different dimensions of God's character and the believer's response to Him. They reveal God as righteous Judge, refuge, Creator, Shepherd, strength, deliverer and King. They also contain significant messianic revelations concerning the suffering and victorious Christ. This study examines these psalms and their implications for personal devotion, Christian leadership, family life, church worship and ministry.

lessonOutline.heading: PART ONE: UNDERSTANDING THE PSALMS OF LAMENT AND PERSONAL DISTRESS

sections.title: 1. PSALM 6 – PRAYER IN A SEASON OF DISTRESS
sections.content:
Psalm 6 is traditionally classified among the seven penitential psalms. The other commonly identified penitential psalms are Psalms 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. It is a prayer of someone experiencing severe distress and appealing to God for mercy. David's prayer reveals that spiritual people are not exempt from emotional pain, physical weakness or seasons of deep discouragement.

A. The Cry for Mercy (Psalm 6:1–3)

David begins: "O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure." – Psalm 6:1 (KJV). He recognises God's authority but appeals to His mercy. His words reveal physical weakness, emotional distress and spiritual anguish. He asks God to heal him because his bones are troubled, and his soul is also troubled. Human suffering can affect the body, mind and spiritual life simultaneously. David's prayer does not establish that every sickness is the result of personal sin. The Bible recognises different causes and experiences of suffering, and sickness must not automatically be interpreted as divine punishment.

B. The Reality of Emotional Exhaustion (Psalm 6:4–7)

David asks God to return and deliver his soul. He describes his emotional condition through the language of tears. Psalm 6:6 says: "I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears." David does not pretend to be emotionally strong when he is hurting. He brings his distress before God. Faith does not require emotional dishonesty. Believers may cry, grieve, express disappointment and acknowledge weakness while maintaining confidence in God.

C. Confidence in God's Response (Psalm 6:8–10)

The psalm changes direction as David declares that God has heard his prayer. His circumstances may not yet have completely changed, but his confidence in God's attention has been renewed.

Practical applications: Do not abandon prayer during emotional distress; express pain honestly before God; do not condemn people experiencing emotional struggles; understand that tears do not necessarily indicate a lack of faith; and encourage people in distress with biblical truth and practical support.

sections.title: 2. PSALM 7 – GOD AS THE RIGHTEOUS JUDGE
sections.content:
Psalm 7 is a prayer for divine justice. David presents his case before God because he believes he is facing unjust accusations and hostility.

A. God as Refuge (Psalm 7:1–2)

David declares his trust in God and compares the danger he faces to the threat of a lion tearing apart its prey. Rather than depending exclusively on his own ability, David seeks refuge in God.

B. The Examination of Personal Integrity (Psalm 7:3–5)

David makes a solemn declaration concerning his innocence in the matter under discussion and is willing for God to examine his conduct. Before demanding justice from others, believers must be willing to submit themselves to God's examination. Christian integrity requires accountability.

C. God Judges the Nations (Psalm 7:6–11)

David calls upon God to arise and judge. Psalm 7:11 declares: "God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day." God's justice is not passive. He sees wickedness and remains morally opposed to oppression, injustice, deception and violence.

D. The Consequences of Wickedness (Psalm 7:12–16)

David describes the destructive nature of wickedness through the imagery of a person digging a pit and falling into it. Evil eventually brings consequences upon those who practise it. This does not guarantee that every wicked person will experience immediate earthly punishment; rather, it establishes the certainty of divine justice.

E. Praise for God's Righteousness (Psalm 7:17)

David concludes by praising the LORD according to His righteousness. Believers should avoid personal revenge, bring unjust accusations before God, maintain integrity under false accusations, trust God's judgment and never celebrate wickedness simply because it appears successful.

lessonOutline.heading: PART TWO: THE MAJESTY OF GOD AND HUMANITY'S PLACE

sections.title: 3. PSALM 8 – THE GLORY OF GOD IN CREATION
sections.content:
Psalm 8 is a hymn of praise celebrating God's majesty and the remarkable position He has given humanity within creation. It begins and ends with the declaration: "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" – Psalm 8:1, 9 (KJV).

A. God's Majesty Is Revealed in Creation

David looks at the heavens and recognises the greatness of God. The moon and stars testify to the glory of their Creator. Creation is not God, but creation reveals the greatness of God. The natural world provides evidence of divine wisdom, order and power.

B. The Remarkable Position of Humanity (Psalm 8:4–6)

David asks: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" He is amazed that the God who created the universe pays attention to humanity. Human beings have been given dignity and responsibility. They are made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour, and entrusted with dominion over the works of God's hands.

C. Dominion and Stewardship

The dominion described in Psalm 8 does not give humanity permission to destroy creation irresponsibly. It establishes human responsibility under God's authority. Human beings are stewards, not ultimate owners. This applies to environmental responsibility, animal welfare, responsible use of natural resources, community development, care for vulnerable people and responsible leadership.

D. The Messianic Significance of Psalm 8

Hebrews 2:5–9 applies Psalm 8 to Jesus Christ. Humanity's intended dominion has not yet been fully realised in the present world. However, Jesus fulfils the purpose of God's design. He experienced suffering and death but was subsequently crowned with glory and honour. Human dignity comes from God's design, and human authority must always operate under His authority.

lessonOutline.heading: PART THREE: THE WICKEDNESS OF HUMANITY AND THE LORD AS REFUGE

sections.title: 4. PSALM 9 – GOD'S JUSTICE AND THE REFUGE OF THE OPPRESSED
sections.content:
Psalm 9 is a thanksgiving psalm celebrating God's righteous judgment and His care for the oppressed.

A. Praise for God's Wonderful Works (Psalm 9:1–4)

David declares that he will praise God with his whole heart. He remembers God's wonderful works and rejoices in His salvation. Remembering divine intervention helps believers develop confidence for present challenges.

B. God as the Righteous Judge (Psalm 9:5–8)

God rebukes the nations and establishes justice. Psalm 9:7–8 teaches that the LORD has established His throne for judgment and will judge the world in righteousness. Human judicial systems may fail, political leaders may become corrupt and powerful individuals may escape earthly consequences, but God's judgment is perfectly righteous.

C. God as a Refuge for the Oppressed (Psalm 9:9–10)

"The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble." – Psalm 9:9. God identifies with those who are oppressed. His people must therefore avoid becoming instruments of oppression. A church that proclaims God's righteousness must also demonstrate concern for people experiencing injustice.

D. Remembering the Needy (Psalm 9:12)

God does not forget the cry of the humble. This should influence Christian ministry towards prisoners, refugees, widows, orphans, victims of violence, people experiencing poverty and those facing discrimination and injustice.

E. The Confidence of the Righteous (Psalm 9:13–20)

David asks God for mercy and deliverance. He concludes by recognising that nations and individuals must remember their human limitations before the sovereign God. God is not merely a source of personal comfort; He is the righteous Judge who defends the oppressed.

sections.title: 5. PSALM 10 – THE APPARENT PROSPERITY OF THE WICKED
sections.content:
Psalm 10 addresses the difficult question of why God sometimes appears distant while wicked people prosper.

A. The Question of Divine Silence (Psalm 10:1)

David asks: "Why standest thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?" This resembles Job's experience. Both Job and David struggle with the apparent delay of divine intervention. Believers may bring difficult questions before God.

B. The Character of the Wicked (Psalm 10:2–11)

The psalm identifies pride, greed, boasting, oppression, deception, violence, rejection of God and exploitation of the vulnerable as characteristics of wicked people. The wicked person behaves as though accountability does not exist. Psalm 10:11 describes his assumption: "God hath forgotten: he hideth his face; he will never see it." This is the arrogance of practical atheism: behaving as though God neither sees nor judges human conduct.

C. God's Intervention (Psalm 10:12–18)

David asks God to arise and defend the helpless. He declares that God sees trouble and grief. Psalm 10:14 says: "Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand." God's apparent silence must not be interpreted as ignorance or approval. Believers must never imitate the wicked simply because their methods appear successful. Success must be measured by faithfulness to God, not by the speed or size of material achievements.

lessonOutline.heading: PART FOUR: THE LORD AS REFUGE, STRENGTH AND FOUNDATION

sections.title: 6. PSALM 11 – TRUSTING GOD WHEN FOUNDATIONS ARE DESTROYED
sections.content:
Psalm 11 examines faith in the face of danger and social instability. David's advisers suggest that he should flee like a bird to the mountain, but he responds by declaring his trust in the LORD.

A. The Crisis of Foundations (Psalm 11:3)

"If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" This question has profound relevance to societies experiencing moral and institutional decline. Foundations may include justice, truth, family stability, integrity, moral responsibility, respect for human dignity and accountability in leadership. When these foundations collapse, society becomes unstable.

B. God's Throne Remains Established (Psalm 11:4)

David responds by looking beyond the crisis. God's throne remains in heaven. The LORD sees and examines humanity. Earthly institutions may collapse, but divine authority remains unchanged.

C. God Examines the Righteous (Psalm 11:5–7)

God tests the righteous and opposes wickedness. The psalm ends by declaring that the righteous will behold His face. When society's foundations are unstable, believers must strengthen their commitment to God's unchanging truth.

sections.title: 7. PSALM 12 – THE POWER OF GOD'S PURE WORD
sections.content:
Psalm 12 describes a society in which truth and faithfulness appear to be disappearing.

A. The Shortage of Faithful People (Psalm 12:1–2)

David cries for help because godly people seem to have disappeared. He describes people who speak with flattering lips and double hearts. The problem is not simply bad language; it is a culture of deception.

B. The Condemnation of Arrogant Speech (Psalm 12:3–4)

The wicked boast about the power of their tongues and believe their words are beyond accountability. This is a warning for leaders, politicians, ministers, employers and public communicators. Words can build or destroy.

C. The Reliability of God's Word (Psalm 12:6)

"The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times." The image of refined silver communicates purity and reliability. Human promises may fail, political statements may change and people may deceive, but God's Word remains trustworthy.

D. The Protection of God (Psalm 12:7–8)

David concludes with confidence in God's preservation. Divine truth must remain the standard in a society characterised by deception.

Practical applications: Be truthful in business, reject false testimony, avoid manipulative speech, do not use religious language to deceive, build relationships on honesty and let God's Word determine your convictions.

sections.title: 8. PSALM 13 – HOW LONG, O LORD?
sections.content:
Psalm 13 is a short but profound lament. David asks "How long?" four times because he is experiencing a prolonged period of distress.

A. The Pain of Delayed Intervention (Psalm 13:1–2)

David feels forgotten, his enemies appear to be gaining the advantage and he is emotionally exhausted. Even mature believers may experience seasons of uncertainty.

B. The Prayer for Divine Intervention (Psalm 13:3–4)

David asks God to consider him, hear him and enlighten his eyes. He does not simply complain; he directs his pain into prayer.

C. The Decision to Trust (Psalm 13:5–6)

The psalm concludes: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." The progression is distress, honest prayer, appeal for help, renewed confidence and praise. Faith does not always remove the question, but it gives believers a reason to continue trusting God while waiting for the answer.

lessonOutline.heading: PART FIVE: REPENTANCE, FORGIVENESS AND RIGHTEOUSNESS

sections.title: 9. PSALM 14 – THE WICKEDNESS OF HUMANITY
sections.content:
Psalm 14 examines the spiritual and moral condition of fallen humanity.

A. The Fool Says There Is No God (Psalm 14:1)

"The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." The word fool describes more than intellectual inability; it describes moral and spiritual rebellion. The person lives as though God has no authority over human behaviour. A practical atheist may verbally acknowledge God's existence while living as though God does not matter.

B. The Universal Corruption of Humanity (Psalm 14:2–3)

The psalm declares that humanity has become corrupt and that none does good independently of God's standard. Romans 3:10–12 quotes this passage, while Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and come short of God's glory.

C. The Need for Salvation (Psalm 14:4–7)

Human beings cannot establish their own righteousness through pride or self-confidence. Salvation must come from God. The passage anticipates the wider biblical revelation of God's redemptive work. The doctrine of human sinfulness must produce humility, not superiority. No person should boast as though naturally better than others. Our hope is in God's grace.

sections.title: 10. PSALM 15 – THE CHARACTER OF THE PERSON WHO MAY DWELL WITH GOD
sections.content:
David asks: "LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill?" The question concerns the character of acceptable worshippers.

A. A Person Who Walks Uprightly (Psalm 15:2)

The person who desires fellowship with God must pursue integrity, righteous conduct, truthfulness and sincerity of heart. Worship cannot be separated from character.

B. A Person Who Controls the Tongue (Psalm 15:3)

The righteous person does not use speech to slander, harm or destroy others. This is a serious lesson for ministers and Christian leaders. A person cannot claim to honour God while using the tongue to destroy reputations through malicious gossip.

C. A Person Who Rejects Wickedness (Psalm 15:4)

The righteous person recognises the difference between those who honour God and those who reject Him. He keeps his commitments even when doing so becomes personally costly.

D. A Person Who Rejects Financial Exploitation (Psalm 15:5)

The passage condemns the abuse of financial power. It rejects lending practices that exploit the vulnerable and accepting financial inducements to pervert justice. Modern leadership applications include refusing to manipulate people financially, sell spiritual influence, accept bribes, make dishonest promises or compromise justice for personal advantage. Genuine worship must produce a transformed lifestyle.

sections.title: 11. PSALM 16 – GOD AS THE PORTION OF THE BELIEVER
sections.content:
Psalm 16 is a psalm of confidence and trust. David declares that his ultimate satisfaction is found in God.

A. God Is His Refuge (Psalm 16:1–2)

David asks God to preserve him and acknowledges that his goodness and security are found in his relationship with God.

B. Rejecting Idolatry (Psalm 16:3–4)

David celebrates the people who belong to God and rejects the worship of other gods. Worship requires exclusive allegiance.

C. God Is His Inheritance (Psalm 16:5–6)

"The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup." David describes God as his ultimate possession. This challenges materialism. A person may possess many things and still lack spiritual satisfaction.

D. Confidence Beyond Death (Psalm 16:8–11)

David expresses confidence that God will not abandon him to the grave. The New Testament gives this passage a significant messianic interpretation. Acts 2:25–32 applies it to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and Acts 13:35–37 also uses it in explaining the resurrection. David died and experienced corruption, but Jesus rose from the dead. God Himself is the greatest inheritance of the believer, and the resurrection of Christ provides the foundation for Christian hope beyond death.

sections.title: 12. PSALM 17 – A PRAYER FOR DIVINE PROTECTION
sections.content:
David asks God to hear his prayer and protect him from enemies.

A. A Prayer for Justice (Psalm 17:1–5)

David appeals to God to examine his heart. He desires to remain faithful to God's Word.

B. God as the Keeper of His People (Psalm 17:6–9)

Psalm 17:8 contains the expression: "Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings." The apple of the eye communicates something extremely precious, while the shadow of God's wings communicates protection and care.

C. The Character of the Enemies (Psalm 17:10–12)

David describes the arrogance and violence of those opposing him.

D. The Hope of Seeing God's Face (Psalm 17:13–15)

David's ultimate confidence is not merely earthly deliverance. He looks forward to satisfaction in God's presence. Divine protection is both a present source of confidence and an expression of God's enduring care for His people.

lessonOutline.heading: PART SIX: THE LORD AS REFUGE AND STRENGTH

sections.title: 13. PSALM 18 – GOD THE DELIVERER AND THE SOURCE OF VICTORY
sections.content:
Psalm 18 is a major thanksgiving psalm and is also recorded in 2 Samuel 22, demonstrating its importance in the biblical account of David's life. David celebrates God's deliverance from his enemies, particularly Saul.

A. David's Description of God (Psalm 18:1–3)

David calls God his strength, rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of his salvation and high tower. These descriptions reveal different dimensions of God's protection. A rock provides stability, a fortress provides security, a shield provides defence and a deliverer rescues from danger.

B. God Responds to Distress (Psalm 18:4–19)

David describes the seriousness of his danger through dramatic images of death, waters, earthquakes and darkness. He then describes God's intervention using imagery of divine power. God is not limited by the magnitude of the crisis.

C. God's Righteousness and David's Integrity (Psalm 18:20–30)

David acknowledges God's faithfulness. These statements must be interpreted in their historical context. David is celebrating God's deliverance in a particular conflict; they do not establish that David was morally perfect. His wider biblical history records his failures and need for repentance.

D. God Trains His Servants (Psalm 18:31–45)

David acknowledges that God equipped him for battle. Divine deliverance does not eliminate human responsibility. God may provide strength, wisdom and ability for the tasks He assigns.

E. Praise for God's Victory (Psalm 18:46–50)

David concludes with thanksgiving, celebrating God's deliverance and covenant faithfulness to him and his descendants. Believers must never claim personal glory for victories that depend upon God's grace. Give God the honour for the strength, wisdom, opportunities and protection He provides.

sections.title: 14. PSALM 19 – CREATION AND THE PERFECTION OF GOD'S WORD
sections.content:
Psalm 19 is one of the most important theological psalms because it brings together two dimensions of divine revelation: God's revelation through creation and God's revelation through His Word.

A. Creation Reveals God's Glory (Psalm 19:1–6)

"The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." – Psalm 19:1. The heavens communicate the glory of their Creator. The regularity of day and night provides a continuous testimony to God's works. Creation does not speak through ordinary human language, yet its testimony reaches throughout the earth. This is often described as general revelation. Romans 1:19–20 develops the same principle.

B. God's Word Reveals His Will (Psalm 19:7–11)

David uses several descriptions of God's Word:

- Law of the LORD: perfect; converts the soul.
- Testimony of the LORD: sure; makes wise the simple.
- Statutes of the LORD: right; rejoice the heart.
- Commandment of the LORD: pure; enlightens the eyes.
- Fear of the LORD: clean; endures for ever.
- Judgments of the LORD: true and righteous; desirable and valuable.

Scripture is not merely a religious reference book. It is God's instruction for human life.

C. The Word Is More Valuable Than Material Wealth

Psalm 19:10 says that God's Word is more desirable than gold. This challenges the tendency to value money above spiritual instruction. A person may become financially successful while spiritually impoverished.

D. The Need for Self-Examination (Psalm 19:12–13)

David asks who can understand his errors. He seeks cleansing from hidden faults and protection from presumptuous sins. This is a prayer for both forgiveness and moral preservation.

E. The Prayer of Acceptable Speech (Psalm 19:14)

"Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer." This is an excellent prayer for every Christian. Our words and inward thoughts must be brought under God's authority. Creation reveals God's greatness, Scripture reveals His instruction, and personal obedience demonstrates our response to His revelation.

lessonOutline.heading: PART SEVEN: THE BLESSEDNESS OF FORGIVENESS

sections.title: 15. PSALM 20 – PRAYER FOR THE KING AND DIVINE HELP
sections.content:
Psalm 20 is a communal prayer for God's protection and victory for the king.

A. Prayer in the Day of Trouble (Psalm 20:1–4)

The people pray that God will answer the king in the day of trouble. They recognise that the king's success must ultimately depend on divine help.

B. Confidence in God's Salvation (Psalm 20:5–6)

The people express confidence that God will save His anointed.

C. The Difference Between Human Power and Divine Trust (Psalm 20:7)

"Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God." Chariots and horses represented military strength in the ancient world. The psalm does not condemn the responsible use of resources or preparation; it condemns misplaced confidence. Human resources are limited, while God remains the ultimate source of security.

Leadership applications: Do not allow money to replace dependence on God, military strength to replace righteousness, human connections to replace divine direction, educational qualifications to replace godly wisdom or organisational structures to replace spiritual integrity.

sections.title: 16. PSALM 21 – THE KING'S JOY IN GOD'S STRENGTH
sections.content:
Psalm 21 continues the royal theme of Psalm 20. While Psalm 20 contains prayers for victory, Psalm 21 celebrates victory received.

A. The King Rejoices in God's Strength (Psalm 21:1–7)

David rejoices because God has answered his requests. His victories and blessings are understood as gifts from God.

B. Divine Judgment Against Wickedness (Psalm 21:8–12)

The psalm speaks about God's judgment upon those who oppose His purposes.

C. Praise for God's Power (Psalm 21:13)

The psalm concludes by calling upon God to be exalted in His strength. Victories should lead to gratitude, not pride. A leader who receives success must remember the God who gives strength.

lessonOutline.heading: PART EIGHT: THE SUFFERING MESSIAH

sections.title: 17. PSALM 22 – THE SUFFERING OF THE MESSIAH
sections.content:
Psalm 22 is one of the most significant messianic psalms in the Old Testament. It describes suffering, humiliation, rejection and eventual deliverance. The New Testament identifies important elements of this psalm with the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.

A. The Cry of Abandonment (Psalm 22:1–2)

"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" These are the opening words of Psalm 22. Jesus quoted them while on the cross. Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 record this cry. Jesus was quoting Scripture rather than expressing a loss of faith. The cry reveals the depth of His suffering and the fulfilment of the scriptural pattern. The crucifixion must be understood within the biblical teaching of Christ bearing sin and enduring judgment on behalf of humanity.

B. The Suffering of the Righteous One (Psalm 22:3–11)

The psalm contrasts the holiness of God with the suffering of the worshipper. The writer remembers God's faithfulness to previous generations and then describes personal humiliation and dependence upon God.

C. Public Mockery and Humiliation (Psalm 22:6–8)

The sufferer is mocked and despised. People challenge him to trust God for deliverance. Matthew 27:39–43 records similar mockery directed at Jesus during His crucifixion, when religious leaders and others challenged Him to come down from the cross.

D. The Physical Suffering of the Messiah (Psalm 22:14–18)

The psalm uses powerful imagery: the sufferer's strength is poured out; his bones are out of joint; his heart is like wax; his strength is dried up; his hands and feet are described in language associated with extreme suffering; his garments are divided; and lots are cast for his clothing. Psalm 22:18 says: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." Matthew 27:35 records the soldiers dividing Jesus' garments and casting lots. John 19:23–24 also records the event and explicitly connects it with Scripture.

E. The Prayer for Deliverance (Psalm 22:19–21)

The sufferer appeals to God for help. This section reflects the movement from distress towards divine intervention.

F. The Transition to Praise (Psalm 22:22–26)

The psalm changes direction. The sufferer begins to praise God among the congregation and declares God's faithfulness to the afflicted. The psalm does not end in humiliation; it moves towards public testimony and worship.

G. The Universal Kingdom of God (Psalm 22:27–31)

The psalm concludes by anticipating the worship of God among the nations. All the ends of the earth are invited to remember and turn to the LORD. The kingdom belongs to God. The suffering of the Messiah is not a defeat of God's purpose; it is central to His redemptive plan.

Theological significance: Psalm 22 reveals the suffering of the righteous, the humiliation of the Messiah, the rejection experienced by Christ, the fulfilment of Scripture in the crucifixion, the movement from suffering to praise and the universal significance of God's salvation.

Interpretative caution: Not every detail of Psalm 22 must be forced into a one-to-one prediction of an event in the crucifixion. The psalm has an original setting of personal suffering, while the New Testament reveals its profound messianic significance. The responsible approach is to identify the specific connections made by the New Testament.

lessonOutline.heading: PART NINE: THE BLESSEDNESS OF FORGIVENESS

sections.title: 18. PSALM 23 – THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD
sections.content:
Psalm 23 is among the most widely recognised passages in Scripture. It reveals God's personal care, provision, guidance, protection and enduring goodness. The imagery is drawn from the relationship between a shepherd and sheep.

A. The Lord as Shepherd (Psalm 23:1)

"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." This opening declaration establishes the relationship between God and the believer. A shepherd assumes responsibility for the welfare of the sheep. The sheep depend upon the shepherd for direction and protection. David identifies God as his Shepherd.

What does it mean that God is our Shepherd?

1. Provision: A shepherd provides for the needs of the sheep. God is the ultimate provider of His people.
2. Direction: Sheep require guidance. Believers need divine direction for daily decisions.
3. Protection: The shepherd watches over the flock. God is the protector of His people.
4. Care: A shepherd recognises the condition of the sheep. God understands our weaknesses and needs.
5. Companionship: The shepherd remains with the sheep. God does not abandon His people.

B. Green Pastures and Still Waters (Psalm 23:2)

"He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Green pastures communicate nourishment and provision. Still waters communicate refreshment and safety. The image suggests a life under the care and guidance of God, but it does not mean believers will never encounter difficult circumstances.

C. Restoration of the Soul (Psalm 23:3)

"He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake." God restores the weary and directs His people in righteousness. God's purpose is not simply to make us comfortable; He leads us into a life that honours His name.

D. The Valley of the Shadow of Death (Psalm 23:4)

"Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me." David does not say that the believer will never enter the valley. He says that God's presence remains even in the valley. Earlier, David speaks about God; now he speaks directly to God. The experience of danger has become an occasion for intimate dependence. The rod and staff represent the shepherd's authority, guidance and protection.

E. The Prepared Table (Psalm 23:5)

"Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies." God's provision is not dependent upon the disappearance of opposition. The presence of enemies does not prevent God from sustaining His people. The anointing with oil communicates honour, care and abundance. The overflowing cup communicates God's generous provision.

F. Goodness and Mercy (Psalm 23:6)

"Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever." The believer's confidence rests in God's continuing faithfulness. The psalm concludes with the hope of enduring fellowship with God.

sections.title: 19. PSALM 23 AND JESUS THE GOOD SHEPHERD
sections.content:
The New Testament develops the shepherd imagery through the ministry of Jesus Christ. In John 10, Jesus identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd.

A. Jesus Knows His Sheep (John 10:3–4)

Jesus describes a relationship characterised by personal knowledge and recognition. The sheep hear His voice and follow Him. Christian discipleship is not merely religious attendance; it involves knowing Christ and responding to His direction.

B. Jesus Gives Life (John 10:10)

Jesus contrasts His mission with the destructive work of the thief. He declares that He has come so that His people may have life abundantly. Abundant life must be understood as life in fellowship with Christ, under His saving and transforming rule. It should not be reduced to material wealth.

C. Jesus Gives His Life for the Sheep (John 10:11)

"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." This distinguishes Jesus from a hired worker who abandons the sheep when danger comes. Christ willingly sacrifices Himself for His people.

D. Jesus Has Authority to Lay Down His Life and Take It Again (John 10:17–18)

This points to His death and resurrection. The Good Shepherd is also the victorious Lord.

Theological conclusion: Psalm 23 reveals the LORD as Shepherd, and John 10 reveals Jesus Christ as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.

Practical applications for Christian leaders: Every pastor, chaplain, teacher and ministry leader should examine their leadership in the light of the Good Shepherd. Do you genuinely care for those entrusted to you? Do you lead people towards Christ or towards yourself? Do you protect vulnerable people? Do you provide spiritual nourishment? Do you remain faithful when ministry becomes difficult? Are you more interested in the sheep or in personal gain? Biblical leadership is shepherding, not exploitation.

lessonOutline.heading: PART TEN: THE LORD AS KING OF GLORY

sections.title: 20. PSALM 24 – THE KING OF GLORY
sections.content:
Psalm 24 is a royal psalm that celebrates God's ownership of creation and His glorious kingship. It has three major movements.

A. God Owns the Earth (Psalm 24:1–2)

"The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." This is a fundamental declaration of divine ownership. Everything belongs to God. Human beings are stewards of what He has created. This challenges materialism, greed and irresponsible use of resources. No person can legitimately claim absolute ownership independent of God.

B. The Character of Acceptable Worshippers (Psalm 24:3–6)

"Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?" The answer identifies clean hands, a pure heart, freedom from vanity and freedom from deceit. Clean hands represent righteous conduct, while a pure heart represents inward sincerity. Acceptable worship involves both outward conduct and inward character. Religious performance cannot replace genuine holiness.

C. The King of Glory (Psalm 24:7–10)

The psalm calls the gates and everlasting doors to lift up their heads. The King of glory is entering. Who is this King of glory? "The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle." The declaration is repeated, emphasising God's supreme authority.

D. The Messianic and Christological Significance

Psalm 24 is primarily a celebration of the LORD's royal majesty. In the wider Christian understanding of Scripture, it is appropriately connected with Christ's exaltation and victorious kingship. However, the psalm should not be reduced to a direct historical description of one specific New Testament event. It gives a broader revelation of the glorious King whose ultimate identity and victory are revealed in Jesus Christ.

sections.title: 21. PSALM 24 AND REVELATION 19:11–16 – CHRIST THE VICTORIOUS KING
sections.content:
Revelation 19 presents Christ as the victorious rider on the white horse. He is called Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords.

A. Christ Comes as the Righteous Judge

Revelation 19:11 describes Him as the One who judges and makes war in righteousness. His authority is not corrupt or selfish. He represents the perfect justice of God.

B. Christ's Universal Authority

Revelation 19:16 identifies Him as "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS." No earthly ruler possesses authority equal to His.

C. The Final Victory of Christ

The passage reveals that evil will not have the final word in human history. Christ will establish His righteous victory. The suffering Messiah of Psalm 22 is also the victorious King whose authority is revealed in Revelation. The cross and the crown must be understood together.

lessonOutline.heading: PART ELEVEN: THE PSALMS OF CONFIDENCE, PRAYER AND RIGHTEOUS LIVING

sections.title: 22. PSALM 25 – GUIDANCE, FORGIVENESS AND COVENANT MERCY
sections.content:
Psalm 25 is an alphabetic acrostic psalm in Hebrew. Its verses are arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, although the pattern is not perfectly preserved in every respect. The psalm is a prayer for guidance, forgiveness and protection.

A. Trusting God (Psalm 25:1–3)

David lifts his soul to God and asks not to be ashamed. He recognises that those who wait upon God will not ultimately be put to shame.

B. Asking God to Teach His Ways (Psalm 25:4–5)

"Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths." David recognises that he needs divine instruction. He does not assume that personal experience alone is sufficient to direct his life.

C. Remembering God's Mercy (Psalm 25:6–7)

David asks God to remember His tender mercies. He also asks that the sins of his youth and transgressions not be remembered against him. This introduces the important relationship between divine mercy and human repentance.

D. God's Goodness and Instruction (Psalm 25:8–10)

God is described as good and upright. He teaches sinners in the way and guides the meek in judgment. Humility is essential for spiritual instruction. Proud people resist correction, while humble people are willing to learn.

E. The Blessedness of Forgiveness (Psalm 25:11)

David appeals to God's name for the forgiveness of his iniquity. He recognises that his sin is great, but God's mercy is greater.

F. The Fear of the LORD (Psalm 25:12–15)

The person who fears God receives divine instruction. God establishes a relationship of guidance and covenant fellowship with those who revere Him.

G. Prayer for Deliverance (Psalm 25:16–22)

David asks God to consider his loneliness, affliction and distress. He concludes by appealing for redemption and deliverance. Spiritual maturity includes the willingness to ask God for guidance, acknowledge personal sin and depend on His mercy.

sections.title: 23. PSALM 26 – INTEGRITY AND THE PURSUIT OF HOLINESS
sections.content:
Psalm 26 is a declaration of integrity and a prayer for divine examination.

A. A Request for Examination (Psalm 26:1–3)

David invites God to examine his heart and inward life. He is not claiming sinless perfection; he is asking God to recognise the integrity of his conduct in the matter under consideration.

B. Separation from Wicked Associations (Psalm 26:4–5)

David declares that he does not associate himself with deceitful and hypocritical people. This does not mean that believers must avoid all contact with sinners. Jesus Himself associated with sinners in order to call them to repentance. The point is that believers must not become partners in wickedness.

C. Clean Hands and Worship (Psalm 26:6–8)

David speaks about washing his hands in innocence and approaching God's altar. The imagery communicates a desire for moral purity in worship.

D. A Commitment to Praise (Psalm 26:9–12)

David asks God not to gather his soul with sinners. He concludes by declaring his intention to walk in integrity and bless the LORD. Worship must be supported by a life of integrity.

sections.title: 24. PSALM 27 – THE LORD IS MY LIGHT AND MY SALVATION
sections.content:
Psalm 27 is one of the strongest expressions of confidence in God.

A. God as Light, Salvation and Strength (Psalm 27:1)

"The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Light means God provides direction and dispels darkness. Salvation means God delivers from danger and destruction. Strength means God sustains His people in weakness.

B. Confidence During Opposition (Psalm 27:2–3)

David declares that even when enemies gather against him, his heart will not fear. His confidence is based on God rather than the numerical strength of his enemies.

C. The Priority of God's Presence (Psalm 27:4)

"One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life." This is one of the most important declarations of spiritual priority in the Psalms. David desires fellowship with God above everything else. His greatest pursuit is not merely victory, wealth or recognition, but the presence of God.

D. The Secret Place of Divine Protection (Psalm 27:5–6)

David expresses confidence that God will hide him in His pavilion. The imagery communicates security and divine preservation.

E. The Prayer for God's Face (Psalm 27:7–12)

David seeks God's attention and direction. He asks God not to abandon him. He also expresses confidence that God will receive him even if human relationships fail.

F. Wait on the LORD (Psalm 27:13–14)

"Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." Waiting on God does not mean laziness or inactivity. It means maintaining confidence, obedience and expectation while depending on God's timing.

Practical applications: Do not make decisions purely from fear; seek God's presence above personal ambition; develop spiritual courage; learn patience; and continue doing what is right while waiting for God's intervention.

sections.title: 25. PSALM 28 – PRAYER, DELIVERANCE AND PRAISE
sections.content:
Psalm 28 is a prayer that moves from urgent petition to thanksgiving.

A. The Fear of Divine Silence (Psalm 28:1–2)

David cries to God and asks Him not to remain silent. He understands that his help must come from the LORD.

B. A Prayer for Justice (Psalm 28:3–5)

David asks God not to treat him like the wicked. He describes people who speak peace while harbouring evil in their hearts. This exposes hypocrisy: people may use pleasant words while practising destructive behaviour.

C. Praise for Answered Prayer (Psalm 28:6–7)

David declares: "Blessed be the LORD, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications." His confidence is renewed. God is his strength and shield.

D. God as the Strength of His People (Psalm 28:8–9)

The psalm concludes with a prayer for God's people. David asks God to save His people, bless His inheritance, feed them and lift them up for ever. The psalm moves beyond personal deliverance to concern for the wider community. Mature prayer does not end with personal needs; it expands into intercession for God's people.

lessonOutline.heading: PART TWELVE: THEOLOGICAL THEMES ACROSS PSALMS 6–28

sections.title: 26. TWELVE MAJOR DOCTRINAL LESSONS
sections.content:
1. God Welcomes Honest Prayer: Psalms 6 and 13 teach that believers can express their pain honestly before God.

2. God Is the Righteous Judge: Psalms 7 and 9 establish that divine justice is perfect.

3. Human Beings Possess God-Given Dignity: Psalm 8 teaches that humanity has a unique position within creation.

4. God Defends the Oppressed: Psalms 9 and 10 reveal God's concern for the vulnerable.

5. God's Authority Is Unchanging: Psalm 11 teaches that God's throne remains established even when human foundations collapse.

6. God's Word Is Pure and Reliable: Psalms 12 and 19 establish the trustworthiness and value of divine revelation.

7. Humanity Needs Salvation: Psalm 14 reveals the universal reality of human sinfulness.

8. Acceptable Worship Requires Integrity: Psalms 15 and 26 connect worship with righteousness and personal character.

9. Forgiveness Is an Expression of Divine Mercy: Psalm 25 teaches that sinners must depend upon God's grace.

10. Jesus Is the Suffering Messiah: Psalm 22 reveals important prophetic connections with Christ's crucifixion.

11. Jesus Is the Good Shepherd: Psalm 23 finds an important New Testament connection in John 10.

12. Jesus Is the Victorious King: Psalm 24 anticipates the glorious kingship that is revealed fully in Christ.

lessonOutline.heading: PART THIRTEEN: THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATIONS – AVOIDING COMMON ERRORS

sections.title: 27. IMPORTANT INTERPRETATIVE CAUTIONS
sections.content:
This section is particularly important for Bible teachers, ministers, chaplains and Christian counsellors.

1. Do not assume that every lament represents a lack of faith. Biblical lament is a legitimate expression of faith.

2. Do not interpret every physical illness as divine punishment. Psalm 6 is a prayer of distress, not a universal explanation of sickness.

3. Do not use Psalm 7 to justify personal revenge. God's role as Judge should encourage believers to pursue justice without taking vengeance into their own hands.

4. Do not interpret human dominion in Psalm 8 as permission for environmental destruction. Dominion involves stewardship and accountability.

5. Do not assume that the wicked always experience immediate earthly judgment. Psalms 9–13 recognise the apparent prosperity of wicked people while affirming God's ultimate justice.

6. Do not use Psalm 15 to teach salvation by human perfection. The psalm describes the character of acceptable worshippers. The wider biblical revelation establishes that salvation is by God's grace and produces transformed conduct.

7. Do not interpret Psalm 19 as teaching that nature alone provides the full knowledge necessary for salvation. Creation reveals God's greatness, while Scripture provides His special revelation.

8. Do not teach that Psalm 22 means Jesus lost His divine nature or ceased to be the Son of God on the cross. His cry reveals the depth of His suffering and His identification with the scriptural language of lament.

9. Do not reduce Psalm 23 to a promise of material prosperity. The Shepherd's provision includes spiritual guidance, protection, restoration and fellowship with God.

10. Do not interpret Psalm 24 as suggesting that outward religious activities can substitute for inward purity. Acceptable worship requires genuine integrity.

11. Do not use Psalm 27:14 to encourage passivity. Waiting on God must be accompanied by faithfulness and obedience.

12. Do not use the imprecatory language of the Psalms to encourage hatred or personal violence. These prayers must be understood within the biblical teaching about divine justice and in the light of Christ's command to love our enemies.

lessonOutline.heading: PART FOURTEEN: PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS FOR CONTEMPORARY CHRISTIAN LIVING

sections.title: 28. WHAT SHOULD THESE PSALMS CHANGE IN OUR LIVES?
sections.content:
A. Personal Spiritual Life

Every believer should develop a lifestyle of consistent prayer, Scripture meditation, genuine repentance, thanksgiving, trust in God, personal holiness, confidence in divine protection and dependence on God's grace.

B. Christian Leadership

Psalm 15 and Psalm 26 should become important passages for examining the character of Christian leaders. A Christian leader must speak truthfully, maintain financial integrity, reject manipulation, protect vulnerable people, honour commitments, avoid hypocrisy, exercise authority responsibly and remain accountable to God.

C. Family Life

Psalms 23 and 27 provide important principles for family devotion. Families should depend on God for provision, seek His direction, pray during difficult seasons, teach children the Word of God, practise forgiveness and build a home around God's presence.

D. Christian Counselling and Chaplaincy

Psalms 6, 13, 17 and 28 are particularly useful when ministering to people in distress. Ministers should allow people to express their pain, encourage honest prayer, provide hope without making false promises, remind people of God's faithfulness, help people pursue forgiveness and righteousness, intercede for people facing oppression and demonstrate compassion.

E. Church Worship

Psalms 19, 23 and 24 should influence the church's understanding of worship. Worship must include reverence for God's holiness, gratitude for His works, submission to His Word, confidence in His provision, personal purity and recognition of Christ's kingship. Worship is not merely singing, dancing or emotional expression; it is the offering of our entire lives to God.

lessonOutline.heading: PART EIGHTEEN: CONCLUSION

sections.title: CONCLUSION
sections.content:
Week 22 presents the Psalms as a school of worship, prayer, righteousness and spiritual maturity. Through these passages, we discover that biblical worship is not limited to joyful singing or public religious activities. It is a relationship with God expressed through faith, obedience, prayer, repentance, gratitude and righteous living.

Psalms 6–13 teach us how to approach God during distress, uncertainty and opposition. Psalms 14–18 reveal the seriousness of human sin, the importance of integrity and the sufficiency of God as refuge and deliverer. Psalm 19 brings together the revelation of God through creation and His Word, establishing Scripture as the foundation for righteous living. Psalms 20–21 teach dependence upon God rather than human power. Psalm 22 reveals the suffering Messiah and its remarkable connections with the crucifixion of Jesus Christ. Psalm 23 presents the LORD as Shepherd, finding a profound New Testament expression in Jesus, the Good Shepherd. Psalm 24 celebrates the King of glory and points us towards the universal kingship of God, ultimately revealed in Christ. Psalms 25–28 return us to the practical foundations of spiritual life: forgiveness, guidance, integrity, courage, prayer and dependence upon God.

The entire study establishes one central truth: God deserves our worship not merely because of what He gives us, but because of who He is. We worship Him in seasons of abundance and seasons of need. We trust Him when the path is clear and when the future is uncertain. We seek His presence when we are strong and when we are weak. We submit to His Word when society accepts it and when society rejects it. And we recognise Jesus Christ as the Good Shepherd, the suffering Messiah and the victorious King.

sections.title: CLOSING PRAYER
sections.content:
1. Father, give me a heart that genuinely worships You in every season of life.
2. Lord, teach me to bring my fears, weaknesses and challenges before You in prayer.
3. Father, deliver me from every form of hypocrisy, deception, pride and unrighteousness.
4. Lord, establish my life upon the unchanging foundation of Your Word.
5. Father, let Your Word continually transform my thoughts, speech and conduct.
6. Lord, be my refuge and strength in every season of adversity.
7. Father, give me the grace to forgive those who have offended me and to walk in integrity.
8. Lord Jesus, Shepherd my life, direct my decisions and restore my soul.
9. Father, make me a faithful shepherd who cares for people rather than exploiting them.
10. Lord, let the revelation of Your glory through creation deepen my reverence for You.
11. Father, help me to remain faithful to Christ even in the face of opposition.
12. Lord, establish Your righteousness in my family, ministry, church and community.
13. Father, let my words and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in Your sight.
14. Lord, strengthen my faith to wait upon You without abandoning obedience.
15. Father, let my life continually proclaim the glory, authority and kingship of Jesus Christ.

In the mighty name of Jesus Christ. Amen.

studies.introduction: The Book of Psalms gives believers a rich picture of what it means to live in fellowship with God. Through praise, lament, thanksgiving, confession, prayer and declarations of trust, the psalmists reveal that worship is not limited to singing or public religious gatherings. It involves the whole life of a person who acknowledges God's holiness, sovereignty, mercy and faithfulness. Psalms 6–28 address the realities of human weakness, sin, distress, opposition, injustice, fear and the need for divine guidance. They also reveal God as Creator, Refuge, Shepherd, Deliverer and King. Within these chapters, Psalm 19 teaches the relationship between God's revelation in creation and His revelation through Scripture; Psalm 22 prophetically portrays the suffering Messiah; Psalm 23 reveals the Lord as Shepherd; and Psalm 24 celebrates the King of Glory. These psalms teach believers to approach God honestly, depend on His protection, pursue righteousness and worship Him with sincere hearts.
